fixtures.city_amends_note: Baltimore City has its own Section 2902 in its building code and its own plumbing code, but both leave the counts as the 2021 model codes print them: Section 2902.1 (the table), 2902.1.1 (calculation), 2902.1.2, 2902.1.3, 2902.2 and 2902.3 are each marked "{As in IBC}", and Sections 401 to 405 and 407 to 426 of the plumbing code are "{As in IPC}". The city's own text in Section 2902 is limited to 2902.1.4 (fixtures in family or assisted-use rooms may count toward either sex in assembly and mercantile occupancies), 2902.4 (signs) and 2902.4.1 (gender-inclusive signs on single-user restrooms). The office, restaurant and school rows of the 2021 table are the same as in the state pack, so its worked examples stand. One difference from the state pack's 2024 text: in the 2021 edition a shared all-gender room must have its urinals in a visually separated area or each in a stall (403.2 exception 6), and urinals in an all-gender room counted on 100% of the occupants must each be in a stall (403.1.1 exception 2).

amendment.text: No change to the counts. City text in Section 2902: family or assisted-use room fixtures may be counted for either sex in assembly and mercantile occupancies; required public facilities carry signs that designate the sex; where separate facilities are not required, a public single-user restroom must be open to any gender and carry gender-inclusive signage.
amendment.quote: Section 2902. Minimum Plumbing Facilities. 2902.1 Minimum number of fixtures. {As in IBC} 2902.1.1 Fixture calculations. {As in IBC} 2902.1.2 Single-user toilet facility and bathing room fixture. {As in IBC} 2902.1.3 Lavatory distribution. {As in IBC} 2902.1.4 Family or assisted-use toilet and bath fixtures. Fixtures located within accessible family or assisted-use toilet and bathing rooms required by the Maryland Accessibility Code (COMAR 09.12.53) are permitted to be included in the number of required fixtures for either the male or female occupants in assembly and mercantile occupancies. 2902.2 to 2902.3 {As in IBC} 2902.4 Signage. Required public facilities must be provided with signs that designate the sex, as required by § 2902.2. Signs must be readily visible and located near the entrance to each toilet facility. Signs for accessible toilet facilities must comply with the Maryland Accessibility Code (COMAR 09.12.53). [...] 2902.5 to 2902.6 {As in IBC}

restrooms_city.rule: Baltimore City Code Article 15, Subtitle 43 (Ordinance 19-265): any public single-user restroom in a commercial or industrial establishment, a place of public accommodation or a City-owned or City-occupied building must be available to individuals of any gender and be identified with gender-inclusive signage (a sign that names no gender, such as "Restroom", "Bathroom" or "Toilet", or a symbol). A public single-user restroom is a single-occupancy restroom for public use with at least one toilet and an outer door the occupant can lock; private restrooms in a residence, apartment, hotel or hospital, and restrooms reached only from a private room or office, are excluded. Enforcement: written warning, then a citation if not corrected within 30 days; a violation is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $500 for each offense, each day a separate offense. The building code repeats the rule at Section 2902.4.1. No city amendment on shared all-gender multi-user rooms: Section 2902.2 is "As in IBC" (2021). Related city rule: Section 1209.4 requires a diaper-changing amenity in every new or renovated assembly, business or mercantile occupancy with a public bathroom (renovations that need no building permit, and places that bar minors, are exempt).
restrooms_city.quote: [Art. 15, § 43-3] Any public single-user restroom in a commercial or industrial establishment, a place of public accommodation, or a City-owned or -occupied building must be: (1) made available for use by individuals of any gender; and (2) identified with gender-inclusive signage. (Ord. 19-265.) [§ 43-1(b)] "Gender-inclusive signage" means a sign identifying a restroom that does not indicate a specific gender, such as "Restroom," "Bathroom", "Toilet", or a symbol indicating the restroom's availability for use by any individual regardless of gender. [§ 43-1(d)] "Public single-user restroom" means a single-occupancy restroom for public use with at least one water closet and with an outer door that can be locked by the occupant. [§ 43-5(a)(1)] A citation under this section may only be issued after the issuance of a written warning and a failure to correct the violation within 30 days of the date of the warning. [§ 43-6(a)] Any person who violates any provision of this subtitle is guilty of a misdemeanor and, on conviction, is subject to a fine of not more than $500 for each offense. [Building Code 1209.4.1] Every new or renovated Assembly Group A, Business Group B, and Mercantile Group M occupancy [...] with at least one public bathroom, and every City-owned or -occupied building with at least one public bathroom, must include a diaper-changing amenity in its public bathrooms, whether designated for men or women or both, or in another appropriate, sanitary space that both men and women can access.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Baltimore job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Baltimore building rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Baltimore offices, hospitals, university buildings and port warehouses, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** Baltimore's building rules require solid plastic (HDPE) partitions to pass a room-corner fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Baltimore's building rules set the number of toilets by how many people use the building. The table below shows what that means.
extra_rule_bullets: - **Changing tables:** a new or renovated restaurant, office, store or similar building in Baltimore with a public restroom must have a diaper-changing station that both men and women can reach. A renovation that needs no building permit is exempt, and so is a place that doesn't admit minors. The city's building official can also exempt a building where a station isn't feasible.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** a Baltimore ordinance requires every one-person public restroom in a business, a place open to the public or a city building to be open to any gender and to carry a sign that names no gender, such as "Restroom", or a symbol. The city gives a written warning first and can issue a citation if the restroom isn't corrected within 30 days. Baltimore's building rules allow a shared all-gender room in place of separate men's and women's rooms if every toilet sits in its own compartment with a door and the urinals are in a visually separate area or each in a stall. Maryland has no state law limiting who may use which restroom, and its public accommodations law bars turning someone away because of gender identity.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Baltimore requires a permit to alter or repair a building and publishes a list of work that needs none. The list covers interior painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, countertops and similar interior finish work, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches. It doesn't name toilet partitions fixed to the floor or wall, so ask the Baltimore City permits office (443-984-1809) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.confirm_office: the Baltimore City permits office at the Department of Housing and Community Development
page.stalls_intro: Baltimore's building rules count toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. It isn't the number of staff or of visitors in a day. Half are counted as men and half as women. Every toilet needs a stall, and every urinal needs a screen on each side. Urinals are optional: in a men's room they may replace up to half of the toilets in an office and up to two thirds in a restaurant or school, so the table shows the men's side as stalls.
page.stalls_after: These are Baltimore's minimums for the whole building, and at least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible. A men's room that needs only one toilet can't swap it for a urinal. An office designed for 25 people or fewer, or any space for 15 or fewer, may have one shared restroom instead of separate men's and women's rooms. A shared all-gender room is counted on everyone in the building instead of half. A restaurant's seasonal outdoor seating counts toward the number of people.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Baltimore's building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20.
page.install_rule: Baltimore requires an installer's contractor license to be registered in the city's ePermits system, using an access code from permit staff, before the contractor is added to a permit. Maryland's state home improvement license covers residential work only. For commercial work a construction license from the Clerk of the Circuit Court, or local county or city registration, may be needed, so installers should check where the job is. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor named on a Baltimore permit must first register their license in the city's ePermits system.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on public projects of $250,000 or more that are run by the State, or where the State pays at least a quarter of the cost, school construction included, Maryland law requires at least the prevailing wage set by the state's Commissioner of Labor and Industry for each county and for Baltimore City. For a carpenter on building work in Baltimore City that is $35.89 an hour plus $14.60 in benefits. Baltimore has its own wage rule for city construction contracts over $5,000: the city's 2026 schedule sets the same $35.89 an hour plus $14.60 in benefits for a carpenter on building work.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 6% in Baltimore. That is Maryland's state rate, and state law doesn't let a city or county add a general sales tax of its own.
page.buyers_extra: - **Hospitals, universities and stadiums:** phenolic or stainless steel where restrooms are cleaned many times a day, HDPE where crowds are hard on stalls.

notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether a like-for-like replacement of anchored toilet partitions in a commercial restroom needs a Baltimore permit (DHCD Permits Office, 443-984-1809, DHCD.Permits@baltimorecity.gov).

Baltimore's own code names the 2021 plumbing code edition, while the State Plumbing Code adopts the most recent version (2024 per a secondary source). The office, restaurant and school counts are the same in both. They differ on urinals in a shared all-gender room: the page gives the city's 2021 wording (a visually separate area or each in a stall). Ask the DHCD Plans Review Office, 410-396-3460, which it applies.

The unamended 2021 model text (fixture table, separate-rooms exceptions, urinal rule) was read on UpCodes' Maryland copy of the 2021 International Plumbing Code: check once on codes.iccsafe.org in a browser. Table 2902.1 of the 2021 International Building Code was not read directly.
Sales tax: the Comptroller of Maryland's rate pages would not open; the 6% rate and the bar on local sales taxes were read in Tax-General sections 11-104 and 11-102 on the General Assembly site.
The city's wage schedule is reissued each year by the Board of Estimates and the state's workbook is reissued through the year: recheck both rates before launch.
Existing buildings in Baltimore follow the Maryland Building Rehabilitation Code for repairs and alterations; how it treats replacement partitions (fire test, permit) was not read.
